::: {.landing-hero}
## Do today's maple seedlings signal tomorrow's saplings?

A forest can contain many seedlings without those seedlings becoming the next
generation of larger trees. This study compares repeated public USDA Forest
Inventory and Analysis (FIA) observations in Michigan to ask what early maple
counts tell us about new saplings recorded several years later.

[Read the research report](report/recruitment.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[Explore the code](https://github.com/dineshpotla/canopy-to-cohort){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}
:::

A forest condition is a mapped part of a plot with similar forest characteristics.
Each paired observation links that area across two visits, typically seven years apart.
Here, a sapling is a tree with a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in
diameter at breast height. It is not a mature canopy tree.

## Three findings to take away

### More seedlings were a useful clue, not a guarantee

Conditions with higher starting counts more often had new maple saplings at
the next visit. But even among the `r high$conditions` conditions with more than
20 seedlings recorded initially, only `r high$conditions_with_new_tally`
(`r scales::percent(high$recruitment_fraction, accuracy = 0.1)`) had a qualifying
new sapling recorded later. Seedling abundance alone does not establish that
the future forest is secure.

![New saplings were recorded more often where the starting seedling count was higher. Bars show the percentage of sampled forest conditions with entry; vertical lines show county-resampling uncertainty. The zero-count group's zero-width interval reflects no observed events, not proof that entry is impossible.](outputs/figures/10_recruitment_counts.png){fig-alt="Recorded entry rises from 0 of 250 conditions without baseline seedlings to 72 of 280 conditions with more than 20 seedlings, or 25.7 percent."}

### Adding more maple measurements did not clearly improve prediction

The study compared models on the same observations, testing each on counties
excluded from its training data. Adding the abundance of existing maple saplings
and larger maples produced small improvements in probability error, but the
uncertainty included both improvement and worsening. These results do not yet
show a dependable advantage over the simpler seedling-count model.

The models account for the area sampled and the time between visits. They are
retrospective comparisons, not a validated tool for prescribing forest treatment.

### Leaving the sapling size class does not always mean dying

A separate check followed 1,580 comparable, previously tagged maple saplings:
1,188 remained live saplings, 334 were recorded dead, and 58 remained alive
after growing to at least 5 inches in trunk diameter. Keeping these outcomes
separate prevents healthy growth from being mistaken for loss.

::: {.feature-row}
## What this means for forest assessment

Seedling counts are worth measuring, but they are one part of the picture.
Repeated visits help distinguish new sapling entry, continued survival,
growth into a larger size class, and recorded death.

No new sapling recorded does **not** by itself mean regeneration has failed.
The inventory samples small areas, seedlings are not individually tagged,
and some entrants may die or grow beyond the studied size class between visits.
These are unweighted results for the study sample, not statewide rates.
:::

## How the question developed

The [earlier detection study](report/index.qmd) examined whether seedlings were
recorded at one visit and not at the next. That is a different question from
whether young trees entered the sapling class. The new study audits repeated
FIA visits and newly recorded stems to examine that transition directly.
It does not claim to follow individual seedlings into individual saplings.

The [research direction](docs/research-direction.md) explains this progression.
The [full report](report/recruitment.qmd) places the analysis alongside existing
FIA research and provides the statistical comparisons, uncertainty, and limitations.

## What remains to be tested

Two possible extensions are documented separately from the completed findings:

- **Seedling length:** a smaller measurement audit suggests a reason to test
  whether taller seedlings add information beyond counts. Only 14 conditions
  in that subset had new saplings, so no added-length prediction claim is made.
  See the [measurement audit](report/ri-audit.qmd) and
  [follow-up study design](report/length-study.qmd).
- **Deer and browsing:** public sources have been assessed, but a suitable
  geographic match and exposure measure remain unresolved. No deer effect has
  been estimated in this study. See the
  [source-feasibility assessment](research/notes/external-factor-feasibility.md).

A [survey-priority comparison](report/recruitment.qmd#survey-priority-comparison)
also tests simple rules against the models. It does not establish fieldwork
benefit or a treatment recommendation.

## Inspect and reproduce

The project includes R code, aggregate evidence, automated checks, and explicit
[analysis decisions](docs/analysis-decisions.md). After obtaining the pinned FIA
snapshot and building the linked cohort, the main analysis runs with:

```bash
make recruitment-core
make test
make report
```

Start with the [reproducibility guide](docs/recruitment-reproducibility.md),
[data dictionary](docs/data-dictionary.md), or
[research evidence](research/README.md). Source data and record-level predictions
are not redistributed. This is a public research draft, not a peer-reviewed
publication or an independently validated management tool.
